content: Newborn infants who are mechanically ventilated and exhibit asynchronous breathing with the ventilator are at an increased risk of experiencing severe barotrauma. This condition can lead to complications such as pneumothorax or intraventricular hemorrhage. Neuromuscular paralysis, which suppresses the infant's spontaneous breathing efforts, allows for complete synchronization with the ventilator and may reduce these risks. However, prolonged use of neuromuscular paralysis in newborns has been associated with potential complications. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether the routine use of neuromuscular paralysis, compared to no routine paralysis, provides clinically significant benefits or harms in newborn infants undergoing mechanical ventilation. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted in multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, EMBASE, and Cinahl, covering studies up to January 2009. References from review articles were also manually searched. The inclusion criteria required randomized or quasi-randomized trials that compared the use of neuromuscular blocking agents during mechanical ventilation to either no paralysis or selective paralysis in newborn infants. Data were collected and analyzed using standardized methods established by the Cochrane Collaboration and its Neonatal Review Group. The quality of the trials was independently assessed, and treatment effects were analyzed using relative risk, risk difference, and weighted mean difference. Out of ten potentially eligible trials, six were included in the review. All the included studies focused on preterm infants with respiratory distress syndrome who were ventilated and received pancuronium as the neuromuscular blocking agent. The analysis of all trials revealed no significant differences in mortality, air leak, or chronic lung disease between the groups. However, there was a significant reduction in intraventricular hemorrhage (IVH) and a trend toward less severe IVH in the group receiving neuromuscular paralysis. In a subgroup analysis of trials involving ventilated infants with evidence of asynchronous respiratory effort, there was a significant reduction in both any-grade and severe intraventricular hemorrhage, as well as a trend toward reduced air leaks. Conversely, in trials involving an unselected population of ventilated infants, no significant differences were observed in any of the outcomes. The authors concluded that for preterm infants on mechanical ventilation who exhibit asynchronous respiratory effort, neuromuscular paralysis with pancuronium appears to have a beneficial effect on reducing intraventricular hemorrhage and possibly pneumothorax. However, there remains uncertainty regarding the long-term pulmonary and neurological effects, as well as the safety of prolonged pancuronium use in ventilated newborns. Additionally, there is no evidence from randomized trials regarding the effects of neuromuscular blocking agents other than pancuronium. Based on the current evidence, the routine use of pancuronium or any other neuromuscular blocking agent in ventilated newborn infants cannot be recommended.
